title: an analysis/reveiw? of Killers of the Flower Moon

commenti.body: I like your analysis and would like to believe there was that level of subtext. I came away from the movie feeling like Ernest just lacked any agency of his own - he loved Mollie when she was physically present, and he deferred to Hale whenever he was there. Hale was essentially a stock gangster character, and Mollie disappeared for most of the second half. It felt like the movie wanted to avoid embellishment in order to be historically accurate, but in doing so it oversimplified the characters to the detriment of the story.

>What we do see alongside the more ‘romantic’ scenes in Killers are the scenes of Ernest robbing the natives and wrecking their graves for jewelry (natives who aren’t directly tied to Mollie). And is it really for the money?  We’re shown that once he gets the jewelry he gambles it all away like it means nothing to him. For a guy like Ernest, it's not only his right to take but his right to lose it like it doesn't matter. He doesn’t want the money, he wants power over people he believes to be lesser than him. 

Such an interesting, interesting point you made here. I didn't gave much thought to the killing and robbery to the Osage from Ernest—such a brutal scene, so short that is almost forgotten, but in a subtle way sets this cold tone for the rest of the film. He wants power, not money, you say... let me mix this with the idea you said about love. 

>I think about the scene when it’s raining , Ernest is closing the windows, Mollie tells him to keep the window open and be quiet, Ernest can’t follow, he can’t keep quiet. It’s really such a simple thing he can't even try to respect on a surface level. And for Mollie this is so much deeper than something surface level, the rain is something powerful for her, Ernest's disrespect ends up causing unnecessary pain for her and probably can’t even begin to understand why. 

I had this impression that Ernest committed some kind of unconscious abuse towards Mollie, which he mistakens as love. He doesn't know what love is, but his morals are so far from anything the viewer and Mollie can imagine, that he believes that following up the orders from his uncle of killing Osage people to end up with the money, isn't much of a cruel attitude, but something logical (he's manipulable too, coming back from war, he'll follow any order coming from his uncle as if he was some kind of officer, perhaps? A "King" as he is called? Probably a way Ernest has of belonging to a family). 

So maybe there's no real love towards her, just the desire of having someone to love, someone to take care of, the desire of having a family — and, of being much more wealthy, and that's where greed gets involved. Ernest acts in selfish, abusive ways. He wants that power, but doesn't even notice. 

Look, I don't have much time, and this answer is all over the place, I'm not even sure of my analysis. I just wanted to continue the discussion, contribute to this post because it's worth is. 

Such a great film, Killers of the Flower Moon. Need to see it again.

ernest was just stupid who couldn't think abstractly. 

"evil comes from failure to think. it defies thought for as soon as thought tries to engage itself with evil and examine the principles from which it originates it is frustrated because it finds nothing in there. That is the banality of evil"

Omg, as a woman of color who's now engaged to the same white man that I loved since before I was really aware of how racism/colonialism affected our relationship dynamics, I interpreted this movie in a very similar way. 

I think with Ernest, he def loved Mollie as much as he could like you said, in a complicated and ignorant way. He loved her like an object, just like his uncle did. To his uncle, the Osage people were like a "special interest" to be fascinated with, learn the language of, and study. But at the end of the day, he still believed that he was above them, so felt entitled to playing with their health and lives. 

There was a scene where he told Ernest something like "I love them, but their time on earth is up, so we need to love them while they're here", implying that Mollie and her family were destined to have been killed in genocide, but weren't because of some fluke in fate. He uses this logic to justify what he believes is his god-given right to rob their wealth. And Ernest "*really* likes money" and idolizes his uncle, so he's empowered to hurt Mollie all the while believing that he sincerely loves her. 

Really great, honest analysis. Thanks for sharing it!!

>I believe that many of the Osage people ended up marrying white men even with the risk of their money being stolen as a form of protection.

I'm commenting again because I like this post so much lol. And I agree with this to an extent, but I think there was also another factor. Mollie kind of assumes that Ernest won't hurt her because he's dumb. She tells her sisters something like "Of course he wants money. But he's not restless, he just wants to relax." She thinks she knows what she's getting into with Ernest (a dumb, lazy guy who just wants to be comfortable and not work), so she feels safe. 

And this similarly happens all the time nowadays in casual sexual relationships between men and women, where both parties think they know what they're getting into, but the differences in societal values and upbringing causes hurt feelings. Mollie and Ernest reminded me so much of situations in which, as a woman, you accept the sexual advances of some dude knowing full well that he just wants you for sex. You feel like you have power and agency because you understand what he wants, until you realize just how little regard he has for you as a human being. You think you're smart, but society doesn't teach women to objectify men the same way it teaches the reverse, so it's ingrained in you to see him as a human and have empathy for him, while he might not (unless he has done a lot of self-reflection and work on himself). Given the way that society values women, it's basically impossible for him to see you as a human being in the same way. So the level of cruelty he can inflict upon you is way higher than what you can inflict upon him, even if you both go into the relationship expecting the same thing. 

I really think this is what happened to Mollie. She was able to see him, a white man, as a full human being, but he wasn't able to see her as a full human being. And this is prob why she was so vulnerable to be fucked over by Ernest, despite being a reasonably intelligent person.
i love this addition!!!! but also feels like a callout bc im kinda going through something like this lmao

>her story was used again for the profit of white people, and that her faith might just be a tool to get money horrifies me that even in death that she and people like her will have to go through that kind of exploitation again and again. I hope that this movie doesn’t end up that way, as another way to find entertainment from her life.

My interpretation of Scorsese's cameo in the coda was that he literally acknowledged the possibility of this criticism being levelled against him, going so far as to depict himself as the ringleader of a show that exploits genocide for entertainment. To me it served as him sort of admitting to that inadequacy in a really interesting and unique moment of self criticism.

I think Ernest loving Molly was also not all chance. I remember a scene where Bill told him about Molly's land and inheritance and Ernest said she might be sweet on him. He kind of went all out in pursuing her after that. Even to convince himself that what he felt for her was love. Or his version of it.

> It felt like the movie wanted to avoid embellishment in order to be historically accurate, but in doing so it oversimplified the characters to the detriment of the story.

I agree that the characters felt really simple, but I think that the movie might be trying to say something with that. That sometimes people might just be caricatures- of evil or of good. It's possible to end up in a location or culture where the strength of its values override any individuals own human impulses, rendering them flat.

All the white folks in the movie are flat, and Mollie becomes flat over time in her marriage to Ernest. Interestingly though, I think Bill and Rita resist this.

I don’t think any of these characters were flat. Hale was convinced he loved the Osage people. He was so devoted to this image of himself as beneficiary and friend of people, even while he knew he was killing them, that he could not give it up, even when told he would not be welcomed back. He really, really thought he was loved unconditionally somehow by these people, that he loved them the same way back. He was obsessed with his own image, not just how he presented himself to others, but also the remarkably deluded way he held himself in his head. 
Ernest does lack a lot of agency, but we can never say he doesn’t make these choices, and remarkably we see a hint in this agency in his “love” for molly. He orders the hit on Henry because he is jealous and angry, he isn’t told to. He chooses to marry her because he is in love with her. He keeps making love with her and gets her pregnant again even though King disapproves. He insists that “no, I married her because I loved her.” He made these decisions.
